title: The orders
hookLine: Qadiri, Naqshbandi, Chishti, Shadhili, Mevlevi and more across the world

cards: A big city has one great mosque at its center, and people walk to it from every direction. Some come down the wide avenue. Some take the back alleys they grew up in.
Some walk slowly, some fast, some sing on the way, some go in silence. They all end up at the same door.

Over the centuries, the chains of Sufi teachers grew into communities with their own names, their own practices, their own personalities, spread from Morocco to Indonesia. Each one is called by a word that means a road.

teach.b: The word is tariqah: a way, a road, a path. Sufis often put it like this: the shari'ah, the law, is the road everyone walks. The tariqah is the way of walking it, with a guide.

And the haqiqah, the reality, is where the road leads. Now, five roads. The Qadiri order, named for 'Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani, a preacher and scholar in Baghdad, with circles from West Africa to South Asia.
The Chishti order, rooted in India through Mu'in al-Din Chishti, buried in Ajmer, known for open kitchens that feed anyone, and for devotional music, qawwali.

The Naqshbandi order, named for Baha' al-Din Naqshband of Bukhara, known for silent remembrance of God, and a phrase: solitude in the crowd, keeping the heart with God while you're busy in the market.
The Shadhili order, from Abu al-Hasan al-Shadhili, in North Africa and Egypt, which teaches its members not to leave their jobs and families, but to find the path inside ordinary life.
And the Mevlevi, Rumi's order, with the turning from two days ago. There are many more: the Tijani across West Africa, the Rifa'i, the Suhrawardi, the Ba 'Alawi of Yemen.

teach.h: LOUD OR QUIET, MUSIC OR NONE.
teach.b: They differ in style, loud or quiet, music or none, withdrawing or staying in the world. Each order would say its own road is a way of following the same Prophet to the same God.

how: Sufi orders, turuq, gather members around a shaykh for teaching, remembrance and service; the Qadiri, Chishti, Naqshbandi, Shadhili, Tijani and others have followers from West Africa to Southeast Asia, and many Muslims belong to no order.

o: a road: a Sufi order and its way of walking
the hidden reality at the end of the path
the law that every Muslim must follow

s: they differ: loud or quiet, music or none. Naqshbandis are known for silent remembrance.
tariqah means a road or a way
the way of walking the road of the shari'ah, with a guide.
the Shadhili order teaches members to leave their jobs
it teaches them to find the path inside ordinary life.

games.q: you're a shopkeeper with a family, drawn to the Sufi path. which road, from today, is known for keeping the heart with God in the busy market?
o: leaving for a desert retreat for life.
the Naqshbandi way: solitude in the crowd.
giving up the shop to turn full time.
games.why: solitude in the crowd: the Naqshbandi phrase for staying inwardly with God while busy in the world.

practice: Of the five roads, which one caught you: the Qadiri, the Chishti with its open kitchen, the Naqshbandi with its solitude in the crowd, the Shadhili in ordinary life, the Mevlevi turning?
Say its name to yourself a few times, and picture its road. If you pray, you can pray for the people walking that road right now.

wordCard.voice: Tariqah. A road; a Sufi order, a way of walking the one path with a guide. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a way, a road; a Sufi order. plural turuq.

carryVoice: Your line: many roads in. Loud or quiet, each one a way of walking. Day three hundred four.
